newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Aid reaches Goma but not its people.
newsitem.headline: Aid reaches Goma but not its people.

text.p: Aid reached the eastern Zairean city of Goma on Monday but not its needy people as international aid teams got bogged down in talks about how to hand out food and medical supplies.

"We were expecting food today. We saw very little, only medicine and a few biscuits. There was no rice, no fish, no meat," complained Laurent Kabila, leader of the rebels who have seized east Zaire's borderland over the last three weeks.

The aid, brought by U.N. and independent aid groups, was the first to reach rebel-held Goma since fighting for the town sent aid workers fleeing nine days ago. It remained packed in trucks parked at the town stadium.
Food riots erupted at the weekend as hungry people fought over the last stocks from the abandoned warehouse of the U.N. refugee agency, UNHCR, in the town.

Security officials from U.N. aid groups met Kabila in Goma to discuss how to distribute the aid brought over the border from Rwanda earlier in the day. The non-governmental organisations (NGOs) hoped to talk to the rebels later.
Another U.N. assessment team also entered the Zairean town of Bukavu to the south, also in rebel hands, on Monday.
Monday's aid will not, however, help the million Rwandan and Burundian refugees who have fled from camps in the area where they lived to the west, across the frontlines.
Kabila said he could guarantee a corridor for the aid agencies up to the frontline but no further.

Up to 400,000 people are believed to be in Mugunga refugee camp just over the battle lines and 15 km (10 miles) from Goma. Armed Hutu rebels, who fled Rwanda after committing genocide against the minority Tutsis there in 1994, are among them.

"People are dying in Mugunga and we have created a safe corridor for NGOs to get to these people. We can guarantee their security as far as our furthest positions but no further," he said in an interview in his fortified Goma villa.

"If we attack the camp to push out killers the international community will start crying again. The solution may be the U.N. can come through our corridors and start negotiating with people in those camps," he added.

Samantha Bolton, a spokeswoman in the Rwandan capital Kigali for Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF-Doctors Without Borders), said the aid trucks got thoroughly searched by rebel forces at the border on their way in.

"They only took in emergency food supplies for patients in hospitals and enough drugs to treat them," she said. "Full-scale operations will only go ahead after they have made their security assessments, in a day or two."
The U.N. World Food Programme, its children's agency UNICEF, the UNHCR, MSF and other aid agencies were involved.
Rwanda on Sunday gave the go ahead for some aid to reach eastern Zaire from its territory but still wants the bulk of aid to go to Rwanda in a bid to coax the refugees to come home.
